examinerBank.question: Walk me through your differential diagnosis for this man's collapse, and how the history helps you rank it.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Top of the list is severe aortic stenosis causing exertional syncope — the collapse occurred specifically during exertion, preceded by chest tightness and breathlessness, fitting the classic triad, and there is a slow-rising pulse and ejection systolic murmur on exam. Cardiac arrhythmia remains important to exclude, especially given his father's sudden death, but the clear exertional trigger and prodrome favour a structural/obstructive cause over a primary electrical one. Vasovagal syncope is less likely as it typically follows situational triggers (prolonged standing, pain, emotional stress) rather than exertion, and usually has a different prodrome (nausea, warmth, visual dimming). Hypertensive heart disease with diastolic dysfunction could contribute to his dyspnoea but doesn't independently explain syncope or the murmur found.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Full marks for ranked list with reasoning linking specific history/exam findings to each differential; partial credit for an unranked or unjustified list.

examinerBank.question: Explain the mechanism by which this man develops syncope specifically on exertion.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: The severely stenosed, calcified aortic valve fixes the outflow resistance from the left ventricle. During exercise, peripheral vasodilation drops systemic vascular resistance in an attempt to increase flow to exercising muscle, but because the valve orifice is fixed and cannot open further, cardiac output cannot rise to match the fall in peripheral resistance. This mismatch causes a fall in blood pressure and cerebral perfusion. Additionally, the high intraventricular pressures generated against the obstruction can activate LV baroreceptors, triggering an inappropriate vasodepressor reflex that worsens the hypotension.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants the fixed-cardiac-output/afterload mismatch mechanism plus ideally the baroreceptor reflex component, not simply 'the heart can't pump enough blood.'

examinerBank.question: His echocardiogram shows a mean gradient of 58 mmHg and valve area of 0.7cm2, with LVEF of 50%. How does this severity grading change your immediate management, and why can't you just start an ACE inhibitor for his hypertension today?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: A mean gradient over 40mmHg and valve area under 1.0cm2 (indexed area <0.6cm2/m2) confirms severe aortic stenosis; combined with his syncope this is a class I indication for urgent valve replacement regardless of LVEF, since LVEF can remain preserved until late in the disease. ACE inhibitors and other vasodilators are avoided or used with extreme caution in severe AS because the fixed outflow obstruction means the heart cannot increase cardiac output to compensate for a drop in systemic vascular resistance — this can precipitate profound hypotension, worsening syncope, or cardiogenic collapse.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Critical-thinking question — wants application of specific echo thresholds to urgency of referral, plus the pharmacological caution rationale, not a generic 'start antihypertensives.'

examinerBank.question: He asks you why he needs an operation instead of just tablets. How would you counsel him, and what happens if he declines surgery?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: I would explain in plain language that his valve has become narrow and stiff with age, and that no tablet can fix a mechanically narrowed valve — only replacing it can relieve the obstruction. I would explain that once symptoms like his fainting spell appear, the outlook without surgery is poor, with a significant risk of sudden death within a year or two if left untreated, whereas valve replacement (surgical or catheter-based) offers a good chance of returning to normal activity. If he declines, I would document his informed refusal, arrange close follow-up, strict avoidance of strenuous exertion, and safety-net him to return immediately with any recurrence of chest pain, breathlessness, or further blackouts.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Assesses communication and honesty about prognosis; should mention the poor natural history of untreated symptomatic severe AS and shared decision-making/safety-netting if surgery declined.

framework: Exertional dyspnoea/collapse syndrome approach: confirm the syndrome (exertional dyspnoea + effort syncope +/- chest pain = triad of severe AS, not diagnosis yet) → localise (LVF pattern vs primary valvular obstruction vs arrhythmic cause of syncope) → grade functional severity (NYHA) → characterise on echo (systolic vs diastolic, valve area/gradient) → identify dominant lesion (aortic stenosis) then any minor lesion → hunt for acute precipitant of decompensation → assess complications (arrhythmia, renal, hepatic congestion) → screen reversible contributors (anaemia, rheumatic disease, thyroid)

patient.name: Mandla Zulu
patient.personality: stoic, downplays his blackout as 'just a dizzy spell', proud of still working in his garden, becomes anxious when syncope is discussed in detail
patient.openingLine: Doctor, I got dizzy while I was digging in my garden and next thing I was on the ground...

presentingComplaint: Collapse with transient loss of consciousness while digging in the garden, preceded by chest tightness and breathlessness

history.fact: The collapse happened 3 days ago while shovelling in the garden in the midday heat; he was unconscious for less than a minute and came round on his own on the ground
Just before he blacked out he felt his chest go tight and became very short of breath, then everything went black
The blackout occurred while he was exerting himself digging; he has had two similar but milder dizzy spells over the past 2 months, both also with activity
He regained consciousness within a minute, was confused for only a few seconds, no tongue biting, no incontinence, no post-ictal drowsiness reported by his wife who witnessed it
For the past 3-4 months he gets breathless walking up his garden path, worse than before; now stops after about 50 metres on the flat
He gets a dull central chest tightness with exertion that goes away with rest, happening more often over the last 2 months
Sleeps propped up on two pillows now, previously slept flat
No episodes of waking up gasping for air at night
Mild ankle swelling by the end of the day for the past month, resolves overnight
No previous history of fainting before these last two months; no seizure history
No history of childhood joint pains, chorea, or rheumatic fever that he recalls
Known hypertensive for 15 years, poorly controlled; no known diabetes; no prior heart attack or stroke
Takes amlodipine 10mg daily, often misses doses because the clinic is far and he runs out; no other regular medication
Tested HIV negative two years ago at a wellness day

Retired farm supervisor, lives with his wife in a rural area near Nongoma, about 40km from the nearest clinic; smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 30 years, quit 10 years ago; drinks a beer occasionally, no heavy alcohol use
Father died suddenly in his 60s, cause unknown; mother had high blood pressure
No fever, no cough, no recent illness, no weight loss, appetite normal, bowel and bladder habits unchanged

examination.general: Elderly man, alert, mildly anxious, no acute distress at rest. No pallor, no cyanosis, no clubbing. No peripheral stigmata of endocarditis.
examination.respiratory: Fine bibasal inspiratory crepitations at both lung bases, clearing partially on deep breath. No wheeze.
examination.cardio: Apex beat sustained and forceful, not displaced, in the 5th intercostal space midclavicular line. Slow-rising, low-volume carotid pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus). Harsh late-peaking ejection systolic murmur, loudest at the right 2nd intercostal space, radiating to the carotids, softer S2 (single second heart sound, A2 not audible). Narrow pulse pressure. No diastolic murmur. JVP not elevated.
examination.abdo: Soft, non-tender, no hepatomegaly, no ascites, no shifting dullness.
examination.neuro: Alert, orientated, no focal deficit, no post-ictal features, no tongue laceration.

investigations.name: Transthoracic echocardiogram
investigations.result: Severely calcified trileaflet aortic valve; peak velocity 4.6 m/s, mean gradient 58 mmHg, aortic valve area 0.7 cm2; concentric LV hypertrophy; LVEF 50%; mild mitral regurgitation; no significant pericardial effusion

investigations.name: ECG
investigations.result: Sinus rhythm, left ventricular hypertrophy with strain pattern (deep S in V1-V2, tall R in V5-V6 with ST depression/T inversion laterally), no arrhythmia captured

investigations.name: Troponin
investigations.result: Mildly elevated at 45 ng/L (upper limit 34), consistent with demand ischaemia from LVH/outflow obstruction rather than acute plaque rupture

investigations.name: Chest X-ray
investigations.result: Cardiomegaly with boot-shaped left ventricular contour, mild upper lobe diversion, no overt alveolar oedema, aortic knuckle calcification suspected

investigations.name: Full blood count
investigations.result: Hb 13.1 g/dL, WCC 6.8, Plt 240 — no anaemia to account for high-output state

investigations.name: U&E and creatinine
investigations.result: Urea 6.2 mmol/L, creatinine 98 µmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L — normal renal function, safe for diuretic/ACEi titration if needed

investigations.name: 24-hour Holter monitor
investigations.result: Sinus rhythm throughout, occasional ventricular ectopics, no significant pauses or arrhythmia during the recorded period

for: exertional syncope preceded by chest tightness and dyspnoea
harsh late-peaking ejection systolic murmur radiating to carotids
slow-rising low-volume pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus)
echo confirms severe calcific AS with valve area 0.7cm2 and mean gradient 58mmHg

differentials.dx: Cardiac arrhythmia (e.g. paroxysmal complete heart block or ventricular tachycardia)
for: father died suddenly, possible arrhythmic family history
against: clear exertional trigger with prodromal chest tightness/dyspnoea typical of outflow obstruction
classic murmur and pulse findings point to a structural valve cause

for: brief loss of consciousness with rapid spontaneous recovery
against: occurred specifically on exertion rather than with typical vasovagal triggers (prolonged standing, pain, emotion)
preceded by chest tightness/dyspnoea rather than typical prodrome of nausea/warmth/visual greying

differentials.dx: Hypertensive heart disease with diastolic dysfunction
against: does not explain the exertional syncope or the specific murmur/pulse character
echo demonstrates a discrete severely stenotic valve as the dominant lesion

pathophys.exertional syncope: The fixed, severely stenosed aortic valve limits the ability of the left ventricle to augment cardiac output during exercise; peripheral vasodilation from exertion drops systemic vascular resistance while cardiac output cannot rise to compensate (fixed afterload obstruction), causing transient cerebral hypoperfusion. Left ventricular baroreceptors may also trigger an inappropriate vasodepressor reflex in response to the high intraventricular pressure generated against the obstruction.
pathophys.exertional chest tightness (angina): Concentric LV hypertrophy increases myocardial oxygen demand while the hypertrophied wall compresses intramural coronary vessels and prolongs systolic ejection time, reducing diastolic coronary filling time; this occurs even without epicardial coronary disease, producing a supply-demand mismatch ('mismatch angina').
pathophys.exertional dyspnoea: Chronic pressure overload leads to concentric LV hypertrophy with impaired ventricular relaxation (diastolic dysfunction); raised LV end-diastolic pressure transmits back to the pulmonary capillaries, increasing hydrostatic pressure and causing exertional pulmonary congestion.
pathophys.slow-rising pulse (pulsus parvus et tard: The stenotic valve orifice prolongs and delays the transmission of the systolic pressure wave into the aorta and peripheral arteries, producing a pulse that rises slowly and reaches a diminished peak amplitude.
pathophys.soft/absent second heart sound (A2): Severe calcification and immobility of the aortic valve leaflets reduce the sudden valve closure that normally generates the aortic component of S2, sometimes leaving only the pulmonary component (P2) audible as a single S2.
pathophys.orthopnoea and mild peripheral oedema: Progressive diastolic dysfunction from LVH raises left-sided filling pressures, which in recumbency are compounded by redistribution of splanchnic and dependent fluid, increasing venous return and pulmonary venous pressure; long-standing elevated left-sided pressures can secondarily raise pulmonary pressures and produce mild right-sided congestive signs.

staging: NYHA class II-III (symptomatic severe aortic stenosis); echo-defined severe AS (valve area <1.0cm2, mean gradient >40mmHg); LVEF preserved at 50%

immediate: Admit for cardiac monitoring given history of exertional syncope with a critical valve lesion — high risk of sudden cardiac death
Avoid strenuous exertion, isometric exercise, and dehydration until definitive management is arranged
Avoid nitrates, ACE inhibitors, and other preload/afterload reducers acutely — these can cause dangerous hypotension in fixed-outflow-obstruction states
Correct hypertension cautiously and gradually only once valve severity is confirmed, avoiding aggressive vasodilation
Continuous ECG monitoring for arrhythmia while inpatient given syncope history
definitive: Urgent cardiology/cardiothoracic surgical referral for aortic valve replacement (surgical AVR) — definitive treatment for severe symptomatic AS
Consider transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) if surgical risk is prohibitive/high, where available and resourced
Coronary angiography prior to valve surgery to assess for concurrent coronary artery disease (routine pre-AVR work-up given his age and risk factors)
Optimise blood pressure control with careful medication choice once valve corrected (avoid aggressive vasodilators pre-operatively)
supportive: Patient education: avoid strenuous exertion and heavy manual labour (e.g. digging, heavy garden work) until valve intervention performed
Salt and fluid moderation appropriate to mild congestive symptoms, avoid over-diuresis which can drop preload dangerously in AS
Address medication adherence barriers — assist with transport/clinic access for chronic antihypertensive collection
Endocarditis prophylaxis counselling if invasive dental/surgical procedures anticipated pre- or post-valve replacement per current guidance
followUp: Serial echocardiography to monitor valve gradient and LV function while awaiting surgery
Cardiology follow-up post-AVR for anticoagulation (if mechanical valve) or antiplatelet management (if bioprosthetic)
Chronic disease clinic follow-up for blood pressure control and cardiovascular risk factor modification
Safety-net counselling: return immediately if further syncope, chest pain, or worsening breathlessness occurs before surgery

stationChecklist.item: Introduces self, confirms patient identity, establishes rapport, obtains consent
Characterises the collapse event fully: onset, context/trigger, prodrome, duration of unconsciousness, recovery, witnessed features (tongue biting, incontinence, post-ictal state)
stationChecklist.answer: Exertional collapse while digging, preceded by chest tightness and dyspnoea, brief LOC, rapid recovery, no seizure features
stationChecklist.why: Confirms true syncope vs seizure and establishes the exertional trigger pattern central to the AS syncope mechanism

stationChecklist.item: Screens for the classic severe AS triad: syncope, angina, exertional dyspnoea
stationChecklist.answer: All three present: exertional syncope, exertional chest tightness relieved by rest, progressive exertional dyspnoea with orthopnoea
stationChecklist.why: These three symptoms define the ominous natural history of severe AS and drive urgency of referral

stationChecklist.item: Takes cardiovascular risk factor history: hypertension, diabetes, smoking, family history of sudden death
stationChecklist.answer: Long-standing poorly controlled hypertension, ex-smoker, father died suddenly
stationChecklist.why: Establishes background cardiovascular risk and possible familial arrhythmic/structural disease to consider in differential

stationChecklist.item: Asks about childhood rheumatic fever/joint pains/chorea as a cause of valve disease
stationChecklist.why: Rheumatic valve disease is a key KZN differential for valvular pathology, must be actively excluded

stationChecklist.item: Explores medication adherence and access to chronic care (distance to clinic, ability to collect medication)
stationChecklist.answer: Poor adherence to amlodipine due to distance from rural home to clinic
stationChecklist.why: Identifies a modifiable precipitant/contributor and social barrier relevant to South African rural care context

stationChecklist.item: Performs focused cardiovascular exam: pulse character, apex beat, auscultation for murmurs, assessment of S2
stationChecklist.answer: Slow-rising low-volume pulse, sustained forceful undisplaced apex, harsh late-peaking ejection systolic murmur radiating to carotids, soft/single S2
stationChecklist.why: These are the classic bedside signs of severe aortic stenosis and directly support the diagnosis

stationChecklist.item: Examines respiratory system for signs of pulmonary congestion
stationChecklist.why: Detects degree of associated diastolic dysfunction/congestion contributing to dyspnoea

stationChecklist.item: Generates a ranked differential for exertional syncope/collapse (severe AS, arrhythmia, vasovagal syncope, hypertensive heart disease) with reasoning for and against each
stationChecklist.why: Demonstrates symptom-to-differential clinical reasoning central to the exam philosophy

stationChecklist.item: Requests ECG, echocardiogram, troponin, and Holter monitor as the key confirmatory and risk-stratifying work-up
stationChecklist.answer: See investigations catalogue — echo confirms severe AS with AVA 0.7cm2, mean gradient 58mmHg
stationChecklist.why: Echocardiography is the key confirmatory test for AS severity; ECG and Holter exclude arrhythmic causes of syncope

stationChecklist.item: Recognises severe symptomatic AS with syncope as a surgical emergency requiring urgent cardiology/cardiothoracic referral for valve replacement, and avoids preload/afterload-reducing agents acutely
stationChecklist.why: Symptomatic severe AS carries a high risk of sudden death without intervention; inappropriate vasodilator use can precipitate collapse
